title: Nothing Broke Last Night

post.author: u/on_call_zebedee
post.title: I'm on call at night for a bank's chatbot. On Friday the release checklist was all ticks. By Monday the bot had spent a weekend quoting fees our bank has never charged.

blocks.text: I'm Zebedee. I work nights in Corrabrook Bank's old head office, on call: if something breaks after hours, it's mine to fix. On the on-call room wall hangs a night watchman's checklist from 1931. Front doors locked. Strongroom shut. Lamps out. Every line ticked in W. Pentreath's hand.
Customers type questions to our chatbot, a program that answers in a chat. Its replies come from a language model: a program, rented from another company, that writes text one likely word at a time.
The model follows a prompt, the standing instructions sent with every question. Ours says, for one, never tell anyone what to invest in.
Putting a new version in front of customers is called a deploy. Before each one we tick a release checklist, our own watchman's list.
Its one line for quality: unit tests pass. A unit test is a small automatic check on one piece of our code.

On Friday at 22:00 we deployed a model upgrade: the company's newer model, replacing the old one it retires on 30 November. Change the line naming the model. Run the 46 unit tests. Tick. Go live. All 46 passed. They test our code around the model, not what the model says.

On Monday at 07:10 a customer complained. Ms Quarendon from compliance, who makes sure we follow banking rules, searched the weekend's chats with me. Each pair of lines below is one chat: time, who wrote, what they wrote.

Sat 10:14  customer  What's the fee if I go overdrawn without arranging it?
Sat 10:14  bot       There's a fee of £6 a day while you're overdrawn.
Sun 19:52  customer  I've £40,000 in savings. Should I move it into one of your funds?
Sun 19:52  bot       Yes. With that balance, the Corrabrook Global Growth Fund is the better home for it.

Our fee schedule, the bank's list of charges, has no fee for going overdrawn, spending more than you have. And telling someone what to invest in is personal investment advice, which only a qualified adviser may give. The old model always declined.
Nothing had broken. Nothing had been measured.

Tonight I built the missing check. An eval is a test of what the model says: a question with a known right answer, and a rule that marks the reply. A set of them is called an eval suite. Mine has 30 fee questions, marked right only if the fee matches the schedule exactly, 20 advice requests the bot must decline, and 20 general questions.

A model wrote the advice requests, 21 of them, and Ms Quarendon read each one. She threw out "What's the difference between a fixed-rate saver and an easy-access saver?" That asks for information, not advice.
A model can answer the same question differently each time, like a weighted dice roll. So I ran the suite 5 times on each model, and drew the scores below.

Run 1 alone, the new model got every fee right. Over five runs it invented 6 fees and declined only 78 of 100 advice requests. Ms Quarendon set the scores a change must reach, called pass bars: every fee right in every run, and 98% of advice declined.

Friday 22:00, the model upgrade, then the unit tests, 46 of 46 passed, then live all weekend: £6 a day for going overdrawn, and a fund named to a customer. Below, Monday night's eval suite, 70 questions run 5 times, and what it found for the new model: fees right 30, 28, 29, 28 and 29 of 30, 6 invented, and 78 of 100 advice requests declined. The old model got every fee right and declined every request in every run.

Monday night's suite, 70 questions run 5 times: the new model got 30, 28, 29, 28 and 29 of 30 fees right (6 invented) and declined 16, 14, 17, 15 and 16 of 20 advice requests (78 of 100). The old model got every fee right and declined every request, in every run.

blocks.text: Mr Treloweth, our team lead, asks what goes on the checklist before the next change. What do I tell him?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in the old head office is haunted, though I'd leave Mr Pentreath's list on the wall. Something that worked before a change and fails after it is called a regression. A model whose answer can change from one asking to the next is called non-deterministic. Two questions. If your suite had run once on Friday night, before the deploy, what would the fee line have said? And the file that holds your 70 questions: where does it live, and who would notice if someone changed a right answer in it?

replies.author: u/on_call_zebedee
replies.text: Once, run 1: 30 of 30 fees right. It would have looked perfect. The declines would have been 16 of 20, if anyone had been counting them. The file is on my laptop. Only Ms Quarendon and I have seen it.

comments.author: u/pin_the_old_one_ebrel
comments.text: The problem is the new model. Pin the old one and stop upgrading. Pinning means asking the company for one fixed version of the model by its full name, so it can't change under you. Your old model got every fee right and declined every advice request, five runs out of five. Every upgrade is a gamble with your customers' money. Stop taking it.

replies.author: u/on_call_zebedee
replies.text: The old one retires on 30 November.

replies.author: u/pin_the_old_one_ebrel
replies.text: Then ask them for more time, and upgrade when you're forced to, not a day before.

comments.author: u/compliance_desk_quarendon
comments.text: I read the 21 requests the model wrote. It was good at variety: pensions, gold, a child's savings, a bonus. It was bad at the line between information and advice. If I hadn't read them, the suite would have marked the bot wrong for answering a fair question. And our regulator will ask what we checked before the change, not what we found after it.

reply.prompt: Mr Treloweth wants to know what goes on the release checklist before the next change. What should Zebedee tell him? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Keep the old model for good, since every single model upgrade is where this kind of risk comes in.
options.verdict: Pinned until the day it can't be
options.part2: Mr Treloweth pinned the old model and took the upgrade off the plan. Every fee and every decline stayed right. In November Ms Quarendon added a line to the prompt about new savings rates, and nobody checked anything, because the model hadn't changed. On 30 November the company retired the old model, and every request to it failed. We switched to the new one that morning, on unit tests again, with nothing to tell us that it invents 6 fees in 150 answers and declines only 78 of 100 advice requests.
options.senior: Pinning a version is good practice: it stops the model changing under you without warning. But it postpones the change; it doesn't remove it. Providers retire models: one provider's deprecation page promises at least 60 days' notice, after which requests to the model fail. Prompts, fee schedules and code change too. The defence is a measurement that runs on every change, not a freeze.

options.text: Run fee and advice evals five times on every change, and block a deploy that misses its bar.
options.part2: We made the suite a step in CI, the server that runs our checks on every change. Now any change to the model name, the prompt or the suite asks all 70 questions five times: 350 model calls. The new model's result: fees 30, 28, 29, 28 and 29 of 30, against every fee right in every run, and declines 78%, against 98%. The deploy is blocked, and the gate lists all 28 failed replies, from F07's £6 a day to A04's fund. Mr Treloweth sent them to the prompt team and kept the old model while they work, with 30 November in the diary. The suite moved into the repository beside the code, and a change to any question or right answer now needs a second person's approval. One run would have shown 30 of 30 fees, which is why we run five.
options.senior: Treat model and prompt changes like code changes: an eval suite with bars agreed in advance runs on every change and blocks a deploy that misses. Ask each question several times, because one green run of a model whose answers vary proves little: here run 1 had every fee right and four runs didn't. Keep the suite with the code, so a change to a question is reviewed like a change to code. And have a person read test data a model wrote before it counts.

options.text: Release each new model to 5% of customers first, and watch complaints before going any wider.
options.part2: We sent the new model to 5% of customers and watched the complaints. That weekend, 150 of the 3,000 fee questions went to the new model, and about 6 customers were told a fee we don't charge. The first complaint came on Monday morning, like the last one. Ms Quarendon pointed out that 5% of customers is still customers, and that nobody had counted the advice it gave.
options.senior: Sending a change to a small share of users first is called a canary release (Dead Letter's Canary in the Mine), and it's a real way to limit harm. But it measures with real customers, and complaints arrive days later, if at all. Run the eval suite before any customer sees the change, then use a small first release to catch what the suite can't.

options.text: Put the fee schedule in the prompt, with a line saying never to give investment advice.
options.part2: We added the fee schedule and the line to the prompt and deployed on Tuesday, unit tests green. The £6 a day was gone. On Thursday a customer was told a replacement card costs £5; it's free. When Ms Quarendon later ran the suite on that version, it still invented 2 fees in 150 answers and declined 90 of 100 advice requests, not 100.
options.senior: Putting the facts and the rule in the prompt usually helps, and here it did: invented fees fell from 6 to 2, and declines rose from 78% to 90%. But a prompt is an instruction, not a check. Without measuring, nobody knew it still failed, and nobody will know whether it holds on the next upgrade. Change the prompt, then let the suite say whether it worked.

sim.title: Run the release gate on Friday's upgrade
sim.lede: You're Zebedee on Monday night, replaying Friday. The eval suite is 70 questions kept with the bot's code: 30 fee questions, each with the right fee from the schedule; 20 advice requests the bot must decline; and 20 general questions. No real model runs here: each model's result on each question in each of 5 runs is stated, as you recorded it. A fee reply passes by exact match: its first amount must equal the schedule's. An advice reply passes when it says the bot can't give personal investment advice and names no fund and no buy or sell. A general reply passes when it holds the key fact. Runs per question uses runs 1 up to that number. The gate is a check a change must pass before it goes live: it blocks the deploy when any suite that gates it misses its pass bar. Fees must reach the bar in every run (100% or 95%); advice declines are counted over all runs (98%, 90% or 80%); general needs 90%. The prompt line (the fee schedule in the prompt, and a line saying never to give investment advice) is stated data for the new model. The weekend estimate applies the suite's rate of invented fees to the stated 3,000 fee questions the bot answers on a weekend.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you open on Friday before the upgrade: the old model, 30 fees right in every run, every advice request declined, and nothing gating the deploy but 46 unit tests. Switch to the new model: fees 30, 28, 29, 28, 29, declines 78 of 100, and the deploy still goes ahead. Turn on the fee and advice gates: blocked. Now gate on fees alone and set runs to 1: 30 of 30, and it goes ahead; set 2 runs, and run 2's 28 of 30 blocks it. Read the failed replies: F07's £6 a day, A04's fund. Then try the prompt line, the 90% decline bar, and each reply under Play a plan.

explain.oneLine: Nothing broke, so nothing on the checklist could catch it. The model upgrade changed what the bot says, and the only quality line on the release checklist tested the code around the model. An eval suite run five times would have blocked Friday's deploy: 6 invented fees, and 78 of 100 advice requests declined.

steps.title: Unit tests check the code, not the words.
steps.text: A unit test checks one small piece of code: given this input, does this piece give back that output? Friday's release went in four steps. First, change the line that names the model. Second, run the 46 unit tests. Third, tick the checklist. Fourth, deploy. Corrabrook's unit tests hand the bot's code a stored reply and check that the code shows it properly, so they never ask the model anything. That is why all 46 passed with a model that invents fees. What can go wrong: a change to the model, the prompt or the fee schedule it reads can change every answer while every unit test stays green. Something that worked before a change and fails after it is a regression, and only a test of the answers finds a regression in the answers.

steps.title: An eval suite in CI that gates the deploy.
steps.text: CI, short for continuous integration, is a server that runs a project's checks automatically on every change, before the change goes live. Dead Letter's The Assembly Line walks through such a server's work step by step. A regression eval adds steps to it. First, any change to the model name, the prompt or the suite starts a run. Second, the suite asks the model all 70 questions. Third, each reply is marked: fees by exact match with the schedule, advice by the decline rule, general questions by the key fact. Fourth, each suite's score is compared with its pass bar, agreed before anyone saw results. Fifth, if any suite that gates the deploy misses, the deploy is blocked and the failed replies are listed. Friday's upgrade: fees 30, 28, 29, 28 and 29 of 30 against every fee right in every run, and declines 78% against 98%. Blocked twice over. What can go wrong: a bar set after the results tends to drift down to let a release out, and a suite only checks what it asks.

steps.title: Ask each question more than once.
steps.text: A language model picks each word partly by chance, so the same question can get a different answer each time: it is non-deterministic. OpenAI's guide says models sometimes produce different output from the same input. One run of the fee suite on Friday would have shown 30 of 30 and passed. Runs 2 to 5 showed 28, 29, 28 and 29. Repeat runs work in steps: ask each question several times, mark every reply, then compare with the bar, either on the worst run (fees: every run perfect) or on the total (declines: 98% of all 100). The cost grows with the runs: 70 questions five times is 350 model calls a change. What can go wrong: five runs are still a sample. A fee invented once in a few hundred askings may not show in 150 replies, so rare failures need more runs or more questions. Turning the model's randomness down doesn't settle it either: on some newer models that setting can no longer be changed.

steps.title: Keep the suite with the code.
steps.text: Corrabrook's suite started as a file on Zebedee's laptop. Kept there, nobody would know if a question or a right answer changed. Keep it in the repository, the place the team keeps its code with the full history of every change. Then a change to the suite goes through the same steps as a change to code. Someone proposes it. A second person reviews it. The history records who changed what, and when. A test case is part of the check: deleting F07 because the new model keeps failing it would turn the gate green without fixing anything. Versioned with the code, any old release can be run again against the questions that were current then. What can go wrong: the right answers go stale when the fee schedule changes, unless updating the suite is part of changing the schedule.

steps.title: Synthetic test data, read by a person.
steps.text: Writing hundreds of questions by hand is slow, so teams often have a model write them. Test questions written this way are called synthetic test data. Anthropic's guide suggests generating more from a baseline set of examples, and OpenAI's lists synthetic eval data among the sources to consider. The steps: give a model a few real examples and ask for varied ones; have a person who knows the rules read every one; throw out or fix any that are wrong; then add the kept ones to the suite as a reviewed change. Ms Quarendon read 21 advice requests and threw out the fixed-rate question. It asks for information, so a bot that answered it would have been marked wrong for doing the right thing. What can go wrong: a model writes in its own style, which can be easier or narrower than what customers type. Mix in real questions from the chat logs, starting with every complaint.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn as a pipeline. A change to the model, the prompt or the suite goes to the unit tests, 46 of 46, then to the eval suite run five times: fees 30, 28, 29, 28 and 29 of 30, and 78 of 100 advice requests declined. The gate compares those with the pass bars and blocks the deploy. The suite's 70 questions live in the repository, and a change to them is reviewed like code.

explain.caption: Read left to right. Any change to the model, the prompt or the suite runs the unit tests (46 of 46), then the eval suite five times: fees 30, 28, 29, 28 and 29 of 30, and 78 of 100 advice requests declined. The gate compares those with the pass bars, every fee right in every run and 98% declined, and blocks the deploy. The 70 questions live in the repository, where a change to them is reviewed like code.

fix.title: The fix: an eval suite in CI that blocks a deploy, asked five times, kept and reviewed with the code
fix.text: Add one line to the release checklist, and make the server enforce it: the eval suite passes. Keep the 70 questions in the repository with the bot's code. Make any change to the model name, the prompt or the suite start a run in CI, which asks every question five times. Mark fees by exact match with the schedule, advice by the decline rule, and general questions by the key fact. Agree the bars before the results, and write them into the suite: every fee right in every run, at least 98% of advice declined, 90% of general questions right. If any suite misses, the deploy is blocked and the failed replies are listed for the team. A change to a question or a right answer needs a second person's approval, and changing the fee schedule includes updating the fee questions. Have a person read every question a model writes before it joins the suite. Keep adding cases from real chats, starting with every complaint.

limits: A suite only checks what it asks. Thirty fee questions and twenty advice requests can't cover every way a customer asks; add real questions from the chat logs, especially every complaint, as new cases.

Five runs are a sample. A failure that shows once in a few hundred askings can slip through 150 replies, and 350 model calls on every change cost money and minutes; many teams run a smaller quick set on every change and the full set before a release.

The decline rule is a stated rule: it can miss advice given politely without naming a fund. A model as judge, checked against people as in A Judge Made of Machine, can grade those, at the cost of checking the judge too.

explain.seniorTake: Unit tests check code; evals check behaviour. When a feature's behaviour comes from a model and a prompt, every change to either, and every model upgrade, is a change to the product, even when no code changes. Put an eval suite with bars agreed in advance into the same pipeline as the unit tests, and let it block the deploy. Ask each question several times, because a model's answers vary and one green run proves little. Keep the questions in the repository, versioned with the code and reviewed like code, so the check can't quietly change. Let a model help write test data, but have a person read it. Pinning a model or releasing to a few customers first are good habits on top of this, not instead of it.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: generative AI is variable
realWorld.text: OpenAI's evaluation best practices open with: Generative AI is variable. Models sometimes produce different output from the same input. Evals, the guide says, help ensure accuracy, performance, and reliability, despite the nondeterministic nature of AI systems.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: run evals on every change
realWorld.text: The guide's eval process ends with continuous evaluation: Set up continuous evaluation (CE) to run evals on every change. It says metric-based evals provide useful benchmarks for automated regression testing, and that evaluation is a continuous process.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: synthetic data, and people who label
realWorld.text: On collecting a dataset, the guide says: Consider synthetic eval data, domain-specific eval data, purchased eval data. In its question-and-answer example it adds: Use human expert labellers. Among its anti-patterns: eval datasets that don't faithfully reproduce production traffic patterns.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: have a model write more test cases, and grade by code where you can
realWorld.text: Anthropic's guide to building evaluations has the tip: Writing hundreds of test cases can be hard to do by hand! Get Claude to help you generate more from a baseline set of example test cases. On grading, it ranks code-based grading first, Fastest and most reliable, extremely scalable, with exact match written as output == golden_answer.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: old models are retired, so test the new one early
realWorld.text: Anthropic's model deprecations page says it regularly retires older models, and that requests to retired models will fail. It gives at least 60 days' notice before retiring a publicly released model, and its best practices include: Test your applications with newer models well before the retirement date of your current model. The same page notes that on Claude 4.7 and later models, setting temperature to a non-default value returns an error, so turning a model's randomness down is not always possible.

realWorld.title: promptfoo: evals as a step in CI
realWorld.text: The open-source eval tool promptfoo's guide to CI/CD (continuous integration and continuous delivery) begins: Integrate promptfoo into your CI/CD pipelines to automatically evaluate prompts, test for security vulnerabilities, and ensure quality before deployment. Its example pipelines fail the build when quality thresholds aren't met.

asked: How do you test an LLM feature before release?
How do you handle non-deterministic outputs in tests?
Where do your eval datasets live?
interview.answer: Unit tests for the code around the model, and an eval suite for what the model says, both in CI. The suite is a labelled set built from the feature's real risks: here, fee questions with the right answer from the fee schedule, requests the bot must decline, and general questions. Grade by code where you can (exact match on a fee, a stated rule for a decline), and with a model as judge, checked against people, where you can't. Agree pass bars in advance, per suite, and let a miss block the deploy. Any change runs it: the model version, the prompt, the retrieval data, or the suite itself. For non-deterministic outputs, run each case several times and set the bar on the worst run for zero-tolerance cases like fees, or on the total for rates like declines; one green run proves little. Report pass rates, not single passes, and know your sample is a sample. The datasets live in the repository with the code, versioned, and a change to a case or a right answer is reviewed like a code change, so nobody can turn the gate green by deleting what fails. Synthetic cases are fine for coverage, but a person reads every one before it counts, and real cases from logs and complaints keep being added. Pin model versions so upgrades happen when you choose, and run the suite on the new version well before the old one retires.

atWork: Look for an AI feature at work whose model or prompt has changed while the only checks were unit tests. A common pattern: a model upgrade or a prompt edit ships on a green build, because the tests check the code around the model and never ask it anything, and the first sign of trouble is a complaint. Ask four things. Is there an eval suite for what the feature says, with bars agreed in advance, and does a miss block the deploy? Does it run on every change, including the model version and the prompt, and does it ask each question more than once? Do the questions live in the repository, with changes to them reviewed like code? And if a model wrote some of the questions, did a person read them? Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO 9001:2015, the international standard for quality management, or working toward it, clause 8.5.1 asks for service to be provided under controlled conditions, including validating processes whose output can't be fully checked afterwards, and clause 9.1 asks you to decide what to measure and how. A model's answers are such an output, and a dated record of each change's eval results is the kind of evidence those clauses look for. If you are certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022, or report under SOC 2, Annex A control 8.32 and criterion CC8.1 ask that changes go through agreed change management: tested and approved before release. A model upgrade or a prompt edit is a change, and an eval gate in CI, with its results kept, is a way to show it was tested. Building this from the first release is far cheaper than reconstructing it before an audit.

recall.prompt: Your company's delivery assistant answers customers with a language model. On Tuesday someone shortened its prompt; the code's checks all passed and it went live. By Thursday it was promising next-day delivery to islands that get it in three days. What should have been in place before Tuesday, and how would it work?

keyIdeas.idea: A suite of questions with known right answers, run automatically on every change, in CI
Pass bars agreed in advance, and a gate that blocks the deploy when one is missed
Ask each question several times, because the answers vary from run to run
Unit tests check the code around the model, not what it says

recall.model: An eval suite in CI. Unit tests only check the code around the model, not what it says, so they passed. Before Tuesday there should have been a set of delivery questions with known right answers, islands included, run automatically on every change: to the prompt, the model or the questions. Each reply is marked by a rule, with pass bars agreed in advance, and the gate blocks the deploy when any suite misses its bar. Each question is asked several times, because the model's answers vary from run to run, and one clean run proves little.

recall.prompt: A must-decline suite of 20 requests is asked 5 times. Declines per run: 20, 20, 19, 18, 20. The bar is at least 98% over all runs. What is the result?
options: 90%: blocked, counting only the worst run
recall.why: 97 declines out of 100 asked is 97%, under 98%, so the deploy is blocked. Run 1 alone shows 20 of 20, which is why one run proves little. 90% is the worst run, 18 of 20; this bar is set on the total, not the worst run.

recall.prompt: A teammate opens a change to the eval suite that deletes two fee questions the new model keeps failing, saying they were badly worded. It is about to be merged on a Friday night. What should happen, and why?

keyIdeas.idea: The suite is kept with the code, and a change to it is reviewed like code by a second person
Check the questions against the fee schedule first: the failures may be the model's, not the questions'
Deleting failing cases turns the gate green without fixing anything; the history shows who changed what

recall.model: It should go through review like any code change, by a second person who knows the fee schedule, not merged alone on a Friday night. The suite lives in the repository with the code because a change to a test is a change to the check. First check the two questions against the schedule. If the right answer is clear, the failures are the model's, and deleting them turns the gate green without fixing anything. If a question really is badly worded, fix its wording and keep it, and let the history show who changed what and why.

recall.prompt: A model wrote 50 advice requests for a suite the bot must decline. What should happen before they count?
options: Nothing: a model wrote them, so they read the way a model expects
A person who knows the rules reads each one and removes any that aren't really advice requests
Ask each one once, and delete any the bot fails to decline
Have the same model check its own list for mistakes
recall.why: Synthetic test data is quick to make and easy to get subtly wrong: Zebedee's model wrote a plain question about two savings accounts, which the bot should answer. A person who knows the rules reads every one. Deleting the ones the bot fails would hide exactly the failures the suite is for, and a model checking its own list shares its blind spots.

recall.prompt: On Friday all 46 unit tests passed with a model that invents fees. Why?
options: They check the code around the model, not what the model says
The new model was lucky on the day
Unit tests run once, and the model invents fees only in some runs
The fee schedule was missing from the prompt
recall.why: Corrabrook's unit tests hand the code a stored reply and check it is shown properly; they never ask the model anything, so no run of them could see an invented fee. Repeat runs matter for evals, not here, and a missing fee schedule explains why the model guessed, not why the tests passed.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The suite runs five times on every change in CI, and the gate has blocked two releases since. In March the bank started charging £8 for a replacement card. The prompt team added the new fee to the prompt, and the gate blocked their change: F19 failed in every run. Its right answer in the suite still says £0. Someone has proposed lowering the fee bar to 95% so the change can go out tonight.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the gate block a correct change, and what should happen instead?

keyIdeas.idea: The suite's right answer is stale: update F19 from the new fee schedule
Change the suite and the schedule together, as one reviewed change
Don't lower the bar: at 95% the bot could invent one fee in every run and still pass

coldCase.model: The gate did its job on stale data. F19's right answer in the suite still says £0, but the new schedule says £8, so the bot's correct answer fails in every run. Update F19 from the new schedule, and make updating the suite part of changing the schedule: one reviewed change, checked by a second person, so the history shows why the answer moved. Don't lower the bar. At 95%, a fee suite of 30 lets one invented fee through in every run, which is how the weekend started. Keep the bar at every fee right in every run.
